blocks.text: 1. overview

blocks.alt: Base models feed a meta-model that produces the final prediction

blocks.text: Bagging combines its many trained models through a fixed rule, a majority vote or a simple average, applied uniformly across every model with no learning involved in how they are combined. Boosting combines its sequential models through weighted summation, with weights determined by each model's own training performance during the boosting process itself. Stacking, short for stacked generalization, introduces a genuinely different, third strategy: rather than combining predictions through any fixed rule at all, it trains an entirely separate model, called a meta-model, whose specific job is to learn how to best combine the predictions of several other models.

This is a meaningfully more flexible idea than either bagging or boosting's combination strategies, since the meta-model can discover subtle, data-driven patterns in exactly when and how much to trust each individual base model, patterns a fixed voting or averaging rule could never capture on its own.
2. Two Layers: Base Models and a Meta-Model

blocks.alt: Layer 1 holds the base models while layer 2 holds the meta-model

blocks.text: Stacking is structured around two distinct layers. The first layer, often called layer 0, consists of several different base models, each trained directly on the original training features exactly as any standalone model would be. Every one of these base models produces its own independent prediction for each training example, using whatever algorithm and approach that particular base model relies on internally.

The second layer, layer 1, consists of a single meta-model, also sometimes called a blender or a combiner, which is trained not on the original features at all, but specifically on the predictions produced by the layer 0 base models, treating those predictions themselves as a new, transformed set of input features. The meta-model's entire job is to learn a mapping from this collection of base-model predictions to the true target, effectively learning which base models to trust, and under which circumstances, rather than treating every base model's opinion as equally important by default.
3. The Value of Diverse Base Models

Bagging and Boosting, the two previous topics, typically combine many copies of the same underlying base learner, many decision trees in Random Forest, many decision stumps in AdaBoost. Stacking works differently in practice: it typically combines several genuinely different kinds of models entirely, for instance a Logistic Regression model, a Random Forest, and an SVM, all trained independently on the exact same training data.

Each of these different model types carries its own distinct inductive bias, its own particular way of finding and representing patterns in the data, exactly the kind of variety already seen across the entire Classification module, a linear boundary from Logistic Regression, a maximum margin from SVM, a set of threshold rules from a tree-based model. Because these different model types tend to make different kinds of errors on different kinds of examples, the meta-model has genuine, complementary information to work with when learning how to combine them, information that combining many near-identical models, as bagging and boosting typically do, simply would not provide.
4. A Critical Pitfall: Data Leakage

blocks.alt: A base model predicting its own training rows causes leakage

blocks.text: A naive, seemingly straightforward way to implement stacking would be to train every base model on the full training data, then simply have each base model predict on that same training data, and feed those predictions directly into the meta-model as its training features. This approach has a serious, easy-to-miss flaw: every base model has already seen the true labels for that exact training data during its own fitting process, so its predictions on that same data tend to be overly optimistic, often far more accurate than that base model would actually be on genuinely new, unseen data.

A meta-model trained on these artificially inflated, leaked predictions ends up learning a badly distorted combination rule, one that may place far too much trust in whichever base model happens to overfit the training data the most, rather than whichever base model genuinely generalizes best. This data leakage problem is subtle, easy to overlook, and genuinely damaging if left unaddressed, which is exactly why a more careful approach, covered in the next section, is the standard, correct way to implement stacking in practice.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: This leakage problem is conceptually similar to, though structurally different from, the target leakage already covered for Target Encoding and CatBoost's Ordered Target Statistics: in every case, a model's own output being contaminated by having already seen the true answer for that exact data point produces misleadingly optimistic results that fail to hold up on genuinely new data.

blocks.text: 5. The Correct Approach: Out-of-Fold Predictions

blocks.alt: Out-of-fold predictions feed the meta-model safely

blocks.text: The standard, correct way to implement stacking avoids the leakage problem directly through cross-validation. The training data is split into K folds, exactly the cross-validation splitting already introduced conceptually earlier in this course and covered in full depth in its own dedicated module later. For each fold, every base model is trained only on the other K minus 1 folds, and then used to predict specifically on the held-out fold it never saw during that particular training run.

Repeating this process across all K folds means every single training example eventually receives a base-model prediction from a version of that base model that genuinely never saw that specific example during its own training, exactly the honest, out-of-sample kind of prediction needed. These out-of-fold predictions, rather than each base model's predictions on data it was directly trained on, become the actual features the meta-model is trained on, eliminating the leakage problem described in the previous section entirely.
6. Choosing the Meta-Model

blocks.alt: A simple meta-model avoids overfitting the stack

blocks.text: The choice of what algorithm to use for the meta-model itself matters directly. A simple meta-model, commonly plain Logistic Regression for a classification stack, is easy to interpret, since its learned coefficients directly reveal roughly how much weight or trust it places on each base model's predictions, and its simplicity makes it naturally resistant to overfitting the combination step itself on top of base models that may already be reasonably complex.

A more complex meta-model, such as a Gradient Boosting model, can in principle learn richer, genuinely non-linear combination rules, capturing situations where, for instance, one base model should be trusted heavily in one region of the feature space and a different base model trusted more heavily in another. This added flexibility comes with a real risk, however: a sufficiently complex meta-model can itself overfit the relatively small, second-layer training signal formed by the base models' predictions, especially since that signal is often lower-dimensional and less rich than the original raw features. A simple, well-regularized meta-model is the standard, safer default starting point in most practical stacking setups.

blocks.text: 7. Stacking versus Simple Voting

blocks.alt: Simple voting uses a fixed rule while stacking learns the combination

blocks.text: It is worth drawing the contrast directly between Stacking and the simpler, fixed voting or averaging strategy already covered for Bagging, and previewed for the dedicated Voting Classifier and Voting Regressor topics coming later in this module. A simple voting scheme treats every base model's prediction as equally important, or assigns fixed, manually chosen weights decided ahead of time, with no mechanism for the combination itself to adapt based on the actual data.

Stacking's meta-model, by contrast, learns the combination weights, and potentially far more nuanced combination rules than weights alone, directly from data. It can discover, for instance, that one particular base model tends to be notably more reliable specifically for one region or pattern within the feature space, while a different base model is more reliable elsewhere, a genuinely more flexible, adaptive combination strategy than any fixed voting rule could express, regardless of how carefully that fixed rule's weights were chosen manually.

blocks.text: 8. The Real Cost of Stacking

blocks.alt: Stacking brings more complexity and training time

blocks.text: Stacking's added flexibility does not come for free. Implementing it correctly, using the out-of-fold cross-validation approach covered earlier in this topic, requires training every single base model multiple times, once per cross-validation fold, plus one final time on the complete training set for use at actual prediction time, and then training the meta-model on top of all of that assembled output.

This makes stacking meaningfully more computationally expensive, in both training time and implementation complexity, than a single standalone model, or even the comparatively simple fixed voting strategies covered in the next two topics of this module. Whether this added cost is genuinely worth paying depends directly on whether the resulting accuracy improvement from combining several genuinely diverse models actually justifies it for the specific problem at hand, a judgment call covered directly in the next section.
9. When Stacking Genuinely Helps

Stacking delivers the most genuine benefit when the base models being combined are truly diverse, meaning they tend to make different kinds of errors on different kinds of examples, exactly the situation described earlier in this topic when several genuinely different algorithm types are combined together. In that situation, the meta-model has real, complementary information available to learn from, since no single base model dominates every situation on its own.

When the base models being combined are instead very similar to each other, tending to make highly correlated errors on the same kinds of examples, there is comparatively little genuinely new information for the meta-model to learn, and the added complexity and computational cost of stacking may not be worth it over a simpler combination strategy. Stacking tends to be reached for most often in settings like machine learning competitions or high-stakes production systems, where even a small additional gain in accuracy is worth meaningfully more implementation and computational effort.
10. Worked Example
The example below builds a stacking ensemble combining three genuinely different base models, using cross-validated out-of-fold predictions to train a simple Logistic Regression meta-model.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import StackingClassifier, RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X = np.vstack([
    rng.normal(loc=[0, 0], scale=2, size=(150, 2)),
    rng.normal(loc=[5, 5], scale=2, size=(150, 2)),
])
y = np.array([0] * 150 + [1] * 150)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42)

base_models = [
    ('logreg', make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression())),
    ('random_forest', RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=42)),
    ('svm', make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(probability=True))),
]

# StackingClassifier internally handles the out-of-fold prediction generation via cv
stacked_model = StackingClassifier(
    estimators=base_models,
    final_estimator=LogisticRegression(),
    cv=5,
)

for name, model in base_models:
    scores = cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=5)
    print(f"{name} alone: CV accuracy = {scores.mean():.3f}")

stacked_scores = cross_val_score(stacked_model, X_train, y_train, cv=5)
print(f"Stacked ensemble: CV accuracy = {stacked_scores.mean():.3f}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: scikit-learn's StackingClassifier handles the out-of-fold prediction generation internally through its cv parameter, implementing exactly the leakage-avoiding approach covered in this topic without requiring the cross-validation splitting to be coded manually.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Stacking trains a meta-model to learn how to best combine several base models' predictions, rather than using a fixed voting or averaging rule.
It structures models into two layers: base models producing predictions, and a meta-model trained on those predictions as its own features.
It typically combines genuinely different kinds of models, unlike bagging and boosting's usual reliance on many copies of one base learner.
Training the meta-model on base models' predictions on their own training data causes serious, easy-to-miss data leakage.
The correct approach uses cross-validated, out-of-fold predictions, so the meta-model only ever sees honest, out-of-sample predictions.
A simple meta-model resists overfitting the combination step; a complex one can learn richer rules but risks its own overfitting.
Stacking's learned combination rule is strictly more flexible than any fixed voting or averaging scheme.
It is meaningfully more computationally expensive, worth it mainly when base models are genuinely diverse and every accuracy gain matters.
Next up: Blending, a simpler, holdout-based alternative to stacking that trades some rigor for implementation simplicity.
